title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1RC---_1LD1LC_1RE0LC_1RF0RE_1RA0RD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1RC---_1LD1LC_1RE0LC_1RF0RE_1RA0RD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The head sweeps the whole tape. The background is the pair 10, and the leftward sweep over it is a proved shift rule. Short walls split it into domains whose lengths near the left end nearly halve one after the other, which suggests a binary counter, but the rule by which the walls move has not been found. Lean proves no halt in the first 10,000 steps by the kernel alone and in the first 107 with native_decide, and proves the shift rules of the sweeps (lean/Rules.lean); the C simulator finds no halt in the first 109 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 36,471 cells have been visited and 18,331 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.521). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.145).

claims.title: Shift rules of the sweeps
claims.text: The leftward sweep over the background: L (10)^n D>1 R and L (01)^n C>0 R cross a whole domain, 2 steps a pair, leaving it as it is, for every n and all tapes L, R.

claims.title: Nearly halving domains
claims.text: Near the left end the domains are about 16674, 4137, 4135, 2065, 1065, 501, ... cells long late in the run; at step 397,048,236 (width 23,150) the first ones are 5316, 1315, 1312, 655, 347, ... pairs. Seen at every end turn; not proved.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The machine halts on B1, reached as A>0 1 (A reads 0, moves right onto a 1). Inside a domain the sweeps never do that; whether a wall ever does is open.

claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RA_1RC0RF_1RD1LE_1RE---_1LF1LE_1RA0LE up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape is the pair 10 repeated, broken by short walls, and the stretches between the walls nearly halve from one to the next, like the digits of a binary counter. Nobody has found the counter's rule.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 36,471 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).
Ratio of consecutive domain lengths near the left end.

sections.heading: Pairs 10 and walls
html: The background is 10 (or 01 in the other phase); the leftward sweep over it is a proved shift rule (lean/Rules.lean). The right end at step 397,048,236 (width 23,150):

sections.heading: Halving
html: The domain lengths near the left end nearly halve: 5316, 1315, 1312, 655, 347, 159, ... pairs here, 16674, 4137, 4135, 2065, 1065, 501, ... cells late in the run (2·109 steps). Toward the right end the tape becomes an irregular mix of short pieces. 1RB0RD_1RC1LE_1LD---_1RF0LE_1LD1LE_1RA0RF of the same batch looks similar.

sections.heading: One pattern at a wall
html: B1 is the only halting transition, reached as A>0 1. Inside a domain this never happens. That a wall never produces it is not known.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.521). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.145).
After 109 steps the tape spans 36,471 cells (24,540 left of the start, 2,334 right), with a density of 1s of 0.503.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A bouncer over the background 10 with many short walls; the domain lengths near the left end come close to halving (16674, 4137, 4135, 2065, 1065, 501, ...), suggesting a counter, but no rule for the walls is known.
family: period-2 bouncer with walls, halving domain lengths
